chapter.title: Hume and Kant: where knowledge comes from

cards.body: If you're 30, you've watched about 11,000 sunrises, and David Hume wants to know what any of them prove about tomorrow. At our long dinner table, Descartes has just said knowledge starts inside the mind. Hume, a Scot writing in the 1700s, leans in and says the opposite: **what we know about the world comes in through the senses**. Then he asks what the senses actually show us.
cards.simpler: If you're 30, you've seen about 11,000 sunrises. David Hume wants to know what any of them prove about tomorrow. Picture a long dinner table. Descartes has just said knowledge starts inside the mind. Hume, a Scot writing in the 1700s, says the opposite: **what we know about the world comes in through the senses**. Then he asks a harder question. What do the senses really show us?

cards.prompt: Hume leans over a billiard table. The white ball rolls into the red one, and the red one shoots off. Using only his eyes, what has he actually seen?

options.text: The white ball forcing the red one to move
White ball moves, the two touch, red ball moves
A law of nature that says balls must do this

whyNot.a: That's the story your mind adds, not what reaches your eyes: the forcing itself is never visible.
whyNot.c: That's a conclusion drawn later, not something seen: no law shows up on the table, only moving balls.

cards.reteach: Describe the scene the way a security camera would. It records movement, contact, then more movement. Anything beyond that, like the push, is something you add.

cards.title: What the senses deliver
cards.body:
Hume's starting rule: every idea in your head began as an *impression*, his word for a vivid first-hand experience, like the heat of a mug, the red of a bus, or a flash of anger.

Now watch the billiard balls again. You see the white ball move. You see them touch. You see the red ball move. **You never see a fourth thing called the cause.**

So why are you sure the red ball will move next time? *Habit*, said Hume. You've seen the pair so often that your mind slides from one to the other on its own.
cards.simpler: Hume's first rule: every idea in your head started as an *impression*, his word for a vivid first-hand experience, like a hot mug, a red bus, or a flash of anger. Picture two billiard balls. The white one moves, they touch, the red one moves. **You never see a fourth thing called the cause.** So why are you sure it will happen again? *Habit*, said Hume. You've seen the pair so often that your mind jumps ahead on its own.

cards.title: Biscuit and the tin opener
cards.body: Every evening at 6, Sam's cat Biscuit hears the tin opener and sprints to the kitchen. She has never once seen the opener cause dinner. She has seen whir, then food, roughly 1,000 times, and **the habit does the rest**. Hume thought animals learn from experience in much the same way we do. Your certainty about tomorrow's sunrise is built like Biscuit's certainty about dinner, just with better vocabulary.
cards.simpler: Every evening at 6, Sam's cat Biscuit hears the tin opener and runs to the kitchen. She has never seen the opener cause dinner. She has only heard the whir and then got food, about 1,000 times, and **the habit does the rest**. Hume thought animals learn from experience much like we do. Your belief that the sun will rise tomorrow is built the same way as Biscuit's belief in dinner. You just have fancier words.

cards.prompt: Your flatmate Jo says: "Coffee wakes me up. I've watched it work every morning for 5 years." Which reply would Hume give?

options.text: You've seen coffee, then feeling awake, about 1,800 times. The 'makes' part is habit joining them.
Five years of mornings is enough to make it certain.
You can't even be sure the coffee exists.

whyNot.b: That's the confidence Hume questioned, not his answer: more repeats make the habit stronger, not the link visible.
whyNot.c: That's Descartes-style doubt, not Hume's point here: Hume's question is what experience shows, not whether the coffee is real.

cards.reteach: Hume doesn't say Jo is mistaken about mornings. He says Jo has seen two things, again and again, side by side. The 'because' joining them comes from Jo's habit, not Jo's eyes.

cards.title: Kant's reply: the glasses
cards.body:
Across the table, in Königsberg, Immanuel Kant read Hume and later said it woke him from his *dogmatic slumber*, meaning years of believing things without checking them. His big reply came in 1781, in the Critique of Pure Reason.

You'd think the mind is an empty screen the senses project onto. Kant said it's more like glasses you can never take off. **Cause and effect is one of the rules the mind brings to every experience**, so nothing reaches you without it.

That wins back certainty, at a price. We know the world as it looks through the glasses, never as it is behind them.
cards.simpler: Kant said reading Hume woke him from his *dogmatic slumber*: years of believing without checking. His answer came in 1781, in the Critique of Pure Reason. The mind isn't a blank screen. It's like glasses you can never take off. **Cause and effect is one of the rules the mind brings to every experience**, so nothing reaches you without it. That wins back certainty, at a cost: we know the world only through the glasses, never behind them.

cards.body: Tom skims a summary and announces at the pub that Hume proved nothing causes anything, so the wine isn't to blame for his headache. Hume never said that; he still expected bread to feed him and fire to burn. **His claim was about what we can see and prove, not whether causes exist.** If a summary says Hume denied causes, it has mixed up seeing with being.
cards.simpler: Tom reads a quick summary and tells everyone at the pub that Hume proved nothing causes anything, so the wine isn't to blame for Tom's headache. Hume never said that. He still expected bread to feed him and fire to burn. **His point was about what we can see and prove, not whether causes exist.** If a summary says Hume denied causes, it has mixed up seeing something with it being real.

cards.prompt: At the long table, Hume and Kant are arguing about cause and effect. Which pair of lines matches each guest?

options.text: Hume: we see causes directly. Kant: causes are just habit.
Hume: cause is a habit built from repeated pairs. Kant: cause is a rule the mind brings to every experience.
Hume: cause is a rule the mind brings. Kant: cause comes in through the senses.

whyNot.a: That's who-said-what scrambled: Hume's whole point is that we never see the cause, and habit is his word, not Kant's.
whyNot.c: That's the two guests swapped: the senses are Hume's starting point, the mind's own rules are Kant's reply.

cards.reteach: Hume starts outside: the senses deliver pairs, and habit links them. Kant starts inside: the mind wears glasses that shape every experience into cause and effect. Same question, answered from opposite ends.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Hume said our knowledge of the world comes through the senses, and nobody ever sees a cause: only the white ball moving, then the red one. So our belief in cause and effect is **habit**, the same kind Biscuit has about the tin opener. Kant answered that the mind isn't an empty screen. It wears glasses you can't take off, and cause and effect is built into the lenses, so every experience already comes with it.
cards.simpler: Hume said our knowledge of the world comes in through the senses. Nobody ever sees a cause, only the white ball moving and then the red one. So our belief in cause and effect is **habit**, like Biscuit and the tin opener. Kant replied that the mind isn't a blank screen. It wears glasses you can't take off, and cause and effect is built into them, so every experience already has it.

cards.body:
Tonight, flick a light switch and say only what you saw and heard: click, then light. Notice the urge to add *because*. Hume would call that urge habit; Kant would say it's the glasses at work. Which sounds right to you?

Tomorrow: Kant says you must not lie, even to a murderer at your door asking where your friend is hiding. Mill would ask what the lie leads to.
cards.simpler: Tonight, flick a light switch. Then say only what you saw and heard, nothing more: a click, then light. Notice how much you want to add one more word: *because*. **Hume would call that urge habit. Kant would say it's the glasses.** Which do you think is right? Tomorrow: Kant says you must not lie, even to a murderer at your door asking where your friend is hiding. Mill would ask what the lie leads to.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now explain, with a billiard ball or a light switch, why Hume said we never see a cause and how Kant answered him.

dubious_claims: 'Everything we know comes in through the senses' overstates Hume: he held that maths and logic ('relations of ideas') are known without experience.
Calling an impression 'a raw delivery from the senses' leaves out Hume's impressions of reflection, meaning inner feelings like anger or desire.
'Hume trusts the senses' (coffee exercise feedback) is shaky: in the Treatise he doubted that we can prove bodies keep existing outside our perception.
Only one of the three exercises tests Kant's reply, so the chapter teaches two ideas but mostly tests one.
repairedFrom.why: The 'In one breath' card only repeats earlier cards in abstract terms, and its teaser for the next chapter is buried in the middle of the chapter, so the chapter actually ends on the try card, which has no hook forward.
repairedFrom.fix: Move the 'Tomorrow' line to the end of the try card and make it a concrete question, e.g. 'Tomorrow: Kant says you must never lie, even to a murderer at your door, and Mill thinks that's mad.'
